2.32 Recreation. The National Park Service administers all recreation on the United States portion of the reservoir area pursuant to a Memorandum of Agreement dated November 11, 1965, between the Park Service and the US Section, IBWC. The area administered by the Park Service is known as the Amistad National Recreation Area and comprises approximately 63,000 acres of land and water. There are no other resources in this region of such quality, capacity, and access to large population centers. Existing recreation use on Amistad Reservoir consists mainly of fishing, boating, picnicking, and general sightseeing. The Texas Parks and Wildlife Department operates the Seminole Canyon State Park under the authority of the Park Service.
Falcon Dam and Reservoir
2.33 General. Falcon Dam, located 84.5 river miles downstream from Laredo, Texas, and Nuevo Laredo, Tamaulipas, Mexico, was the first international storage dam constructed under the 1944 Water Treaty. Construction started December 15, 1950 and was completed on April 8, 1954. The 4.98 mile long earth filled structure has a maximum height of 150 feet above the riverbed. At its conservation pool elevation of 301.2 feet above sea level, the lake has an area of 87,000 surface acres with a capacity of 2,668,000 acre-feet. The Falcon Dam and Power Plant provides for control of flood waters, storage of water for conservation purposes, recreation, and generation of hydroelectric power.
2.34 The United States and Mexico have each constructed hydroelectric power plants near the downstream toe of the dam which are identical in size, generating and service equipment, and facilities for servicing. Each plant contains three vertical-shaft, single runner, Francis type turbines rated at 14,750 horsepower output at 100 feet net head and at a speed of 163.6 revolutions per minute. The power operating head varies from 65 to 123 feet on the United States plant. Each turbine is directly connected to a generator rated at 10,500 kilowatts, 6,900 volts. Each plant has a centralized control room with separate and independent facilities and the two plants are electrically interconnected for transfer of electric energy. In accordance with the 1944 Water Treaty, the energy generated by both power plants is divided equally between the United States and Mexico. Energy is generated only when releases are being made for municipal and irrigation uses, and for flood operations. Falcon power is not dependable due to the unpredictable pattern of reservoir releases.
2.35 The United States power outlets consist of four 13-foot penstocks, through three of which water is admitted to the turbines. Water may bypass the turbines to the river channel below through two 72-inch hollow jet valves which branch from the number one penstock. The fourth penstock allows for future installation of an additional generating unit. The water enters the penstock at centerline elevation 231.5 feet and enters the turbines at centerline elevation 186.0 feet. The United States share of energy, in excess of project needs, is sold to Central Power and Light Company.
2.36 The Mexican power outlet consists of one 22-foot diameter penstock, with the upper end located in a conventional type tower structure. At the lower end, the single penstock subdivides into a manifold section with the water passing through three 13-foot diameter penstocks to the turbines. The turbine may be bypassed to the river channel through two 90-inch bypass lines. A fourth 13-foot penstock branches off the manifold to allow for further installation of a fourth generating unit. The water enters the 22-foot penstock at centerline elevation 223.35 feet and enters the turbine at centerline elevation 186.0 feet.
